historical_timeline.summary: Born prematurely in Saint Bethlehem, near Clarksville, Tennessee, weighing about 4.5 pounds.
Double pneumonia and scarlet fever at about four; polio in early childhood leaves the left leg partly paralyzed.
Wears a metal leg brace and special shoe; weekly treatment at Meharry Medical College in Nashville, with massage at home.
Walks without the brace by about twelve, after taking it off in public at about nine and a half.
Wins a bronze medal in the 4 x 100-meter relay at the Melbourne Olympics, at sixteen.
Wins three gold medals at the Rome Olympics: 100 meters, 200 meters and the 4 x 100-meter relay.
Returns to Tennessee as a vice president of a Nashville hospital.
Dies of brain cancer at her home in Brentwood, Tennessee, at 54, after a diagnosis earlier that year, reported shortly after her mother's death.

claims.statement: She wore a metal leg brace for several years (from about age six to ten in one account) and a specially made shoe. Once a week her mother took her by bus to Nashville, a 90-minute round trip, to the closest doctors who would treat her in the segregated South: physicians at Meharry Medical College, a historically Black medical school, fitted the brace and prescribed massage and heat. At home her family massaged the leg several times a day.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern equity teaching: as a child she had to travel to a Black medical school for care that was not offered to her nearer home.

claims.statement: At sixteen she won a bronze medal in the 4 x 100-meter relay at the 1956 Olympic Games in Melbourne. At the 1960 Games in Rome she won gold in the 100 meters, the 200 meters and the 4 x 100-meter relay, the first American woman to win three gold medals in track and field at one Olympics. She ran for the Tennessee State University Tigerbelles.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize new progressive neurologic symptoms (morning headache, word-finding pauses and a clumsy hand) as a reason for prompt contrast MRI of the brain in a 54-year-old Black woman who survived childhood polio, and then manage a newly diagnosed glioblastoma to current standards: dexamethasone only for symptomatic edema, at the lowest dose and tapered early, with glucose and stomach protection; no seizure prophylaxis when no seizure has occurred; CT to exclude another primary; awake craniotomy with language and motor mapping for maximal safe resection and an MRI within 48 hours; the WHO CNS5 1989 integrated diagnosis with IDH, TERT, EGFR, chromosome 7 and 10 and MGMT promoter methylation; radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide and Pneumocystis prophylaxis, then adjuvant temozolomide with tumor-treating fields; blood count and liver test monitoring; RANO 2.0 response assessment that allows for pseudoprogression; venous thromboembolism awareness; fall prevention for a woman whose new right-sided weakness meets a left leg weakened by polio in childhood; and early palliative care with advance care planning alongside treatment, on the NCCN CNS cancers guideline, the EANO 1989 diffuse glioma guideline and the ASCO-SNO glioma guideline. Her childhood care, given at a Black medical school because care nearer home was not offered to her, frames the commitment to equal access to a brain tumor center and clinical trials.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Rudolph returns three days after her first visit. The MRI the next morning showed a 3.8 cm ring-enhancing mass in the left posterior frontal lobe with central necrosis, surrounding edema and 5 mm of midline shift. Dr. Haynes-Whitaker telephoned her the same afternoon and started dexamethasone 4 mg twice a day with famotidine. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis yesterday showed no cancer elsewhere. She has had no seizure, vomiting or drowsiness. She saw Dr. Brzezinski of neuro-oncology this morning, together with the neurosurgery team. She is not driving. She said that as a child she was told she would never walk, and that she wants the facts as they are. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Rudolph returns three weeks after an awake left frontal craniotomy. The surgeons removed all of the enhancing tumor, stopping at the mapped language sites, and the MRI the next day showed no residual enhancing tumor. Her speech was slower for three days after surgery and then came back to normal; she went home on the third day, having had heparin injections in hospital to prevent clots. She has had no seizure. The right hand is nearly back to normal, though fine buttons are still slow. The physical therapist saw her a week ago and gave her a home exercise program and a cane for uneven ground. She is now on dexamethasone 2 mg twice a day. Her fingerstick glucose readings at home have been 140 to 180 mg/dL after meals, and she is thirsty in the evenings. The pathology is glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, with MGMT promoter methylation, and the tumor board has reviewed it with Dr. Brzezinski. She has met the radiation oncologist and had her planning scan, and starts radiotherapy with temozolomide on Monday. She has had no thoughts of self-harm.

assessment.assessment: A single necrotic ring-enhancing mass with raised perfusion in a woman of 54 without cancer elsewhere on CT is most likely a glioblastoma. A solitary metastasis has been made unlikely by the CT; lymphoma would usually enhance solidly and restrict diffusion; an abscess would restrict diffusion in its center. The mass sits just behind the expressive language area and in front of the motor strip, and the edema explains much of her symptoms. Maximal safe resection, rather than biopsy alone, gives the tissue diagnosis, relieves the mass effect and improves survival, and an awake craniotomy with cortical and subcortical language and motor mapping lets the surgeons remove the tumor while protecting speech and hand function. A functional MRI with tractography beforehand will show the language areas and the motor tract. The tissue needs an integrated WHO CNS5 diagnosis: IDH1 R132H immunostaining, with IDH1 and IDH2 sequencing if it is negative because she is 54, ATRX and p53, the TERT promoter, EGFR amplification and chromosome 7 gain with 10 loss, which define glioblastoma when IDH is wild-type, CDKN2A, histone H3 and BRAF, and MGMT promoter methylation, which predicts benefit from temozolomide. If this is a glioblastoma, the standard after surgery is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide 75 mg/m2, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and weekly blood counts, then six cycles of adjuvant temozolomide, with tumor-treating fields offered for the adjuvant phase, and screening for a clinical trial. Dexamethasone is right for edema causing symptoms and should be tapered as soon as possible after surgery. She has had no seizure, so she should not have a prophylactic antiseizure drug. Brain tumors carry a high risk of venous thromboembolism: she needs mechanical and then heparin prophylaxis in hospital after surgery, but not routinely at home
